tour.title: Fira to Oia: The Caldera Rim Walk
tour.summary: The classic caldera-rim hike, walked north from the working capital to the postcard village — eleven kilometres of cliff path over one volcano, one buried Bronze Age town, and a sunset the world decided to buy.
tour.overviewText:
Santorini is the rim of a volcano that blew itself apart. The bay you will walk around is a caldera — the collapsed crater of one of the largest eruptions in human history — and the white villages on its lip are built from the same ash and pumice it threw out roughly three and a half thousand years ago. Every view on this walk is a view down into that crater.

The eruption happened around 1600 BC. The island was then a ring of land around a bay, with a Bronze Age town at Akrotiri on the south coast. Ash and pumice buried the town so completely that its frescoes and three-storey houses survive; the inhabitants had already fled, warned by earthquakes, and no bodies have ever been found. The centre of the island then collapsed into the sea and left the crescent you see. So this landscape is not scenery: it is the event, and the vineyards, the cliffs and the villages all sit on what the volcano left behind.

Greece is overwhelmingly Greek Orthodox, and Santorini also carries a small Catholic community left by nearly four centuries of Venetian rule: the island still has its own Catholic diocese, and its most photographed church, the Three Bells, is Catholic. The economy is tourism, and the argument about it is unresolved. Around two million people visit a year against roughly fifteen thousand residents, and in summer cruise ships anchor in the caldera and send thousands of day-trippers up the cliff at once. Since 2025 Greece has charged cruise passengers a fee of up to €20 to come ashore here in peak season, and the island has moved to cap cruise arrivals at about 8,000 a day. Supporters call that a start; critics say it is far too little, and point at water: there are no rivers here, desalinated tap water is salty, and every pool on the cliff must be supplied by plant or tanker. Meanwhile the cliffs themselves are being loaded with cave rooms and pools, and in August 2025 a section of cliff beside a hotel under construction in Imerovigli gave way.

The route is a single line north along the caldera rim: out of Fira, through Firostefani and Imerovigli, past the Venetian fortress rock of Skaros and a chapel on the ridge, then along the exposed northern cliff path into Oia, finishing at the castle ruins as the sun goes down. The first half is paved village lanes and steps; the second half is dirt and loose volcanic gravel with almost no shade. It is about eleven kilometres, and a full day at an unhurried pace.

Start early — in mid-September the sun is still fierce by ten — and carry at least 1.5 litres of water each: there is no water and no shade after Imerovigli. Wear shoes with grip, not flip-flops, and do not trust a mapping app in Fira or Imerovigli, which will route you inland along the main road. Imerovigli is the last reliable shop, toilet and café before Oia. Buses run from Oia back to Fira late into the evening, but the queue after sunset is long.

Go north, go early, and you will have the caldera to yourself for the first hour — which is when it is worth having.
tour.difficulty: Moderate. Roughly eleven kilometres of paved village lanes, steps, cobbles, dirt and loose volcanic gravel, with several real climbs and almost no shade after Imerovigli. No technical hiking, but the footing is bad in places and the path runs beside unprotected drops; the Skaros Rock detour adds an hour of steep steps on top.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at first light, around 07:00 in mid-September, from Fira. You get the rim path to yourself for the first hour, the heat has not arrived, and you reach Oia in the late afternoon with time to eat before the sunset. Do not attempt the exposed middle section after dark, and do not try to walk back to Fira after sunset — take the bus.

stops.name: Fira Main Square (Plateia Theotokopoulou)
stops.narration:
Start in the square, because Fira is where this island actually works. This is Plateia Theotokopoulou, the main square, named for the family name of Domenikos Theotokopoulos — El Greco — the Cretan-born painter the world knows by that nickname. Around you are the bus station, the taxis, the banks and the pharmacies: Fira is the administrative capital of Thira, which is the island's official name. Santorini is a contraction of Santa Irini, Saint Irene, first written down by the Arab geographer al-Idrisi around 1154, and the nickname outlived the official name.

About fifteen thousand people live on the whole island; roughly two million visit it in a year. That ratio is Santorini's whole story, and you are standing where it is most visible, because this square sits at the top of the cliff that the cruise ships climb.

Walk to the caldera edge and look down. At the bottom is the Old Port, Gialos, and above it a switchback of some six hundred steps. Until 1982 the only ways up were those steps, a donkey, or a mule — and the animals carried everything: luggage, cement, tourists, for a fee negotiated on the spot. There is a real animal-welfare problem in that trade, because donkeys work in heat, on stone, under heavy loads. The cable car was built to take the pressure off. It was paid for by the Loula and Evangelos Nomikos Foundation, opened in 1982, climbs 220 metres in three to five minutes, and cost about €10 one way in 2025, half that for children. A share of every ticket goes to the island's fourteen communities and specifically to support the mule drivers, which is a neat way of paying off a tradition without abolishing it. Verify the fare at the gate; it moves.

Now the harder subject, stated plainly: water. Santorini has no rivers, no lakes, and a few hundred millimetres of rain a year, almost all of it between November and March. Islanders used to catch the winter rain off their roofs into cisterns cut into the rock. Tourism outgrew that, so since the 1990s the island has run desalination plants — the first at Oia, in 1992 — and the tap water is drinkable but noticeably salty. Most people drink bottled, and the bottles are the second problem. When you see a swimming pool hanging on the caldera edge, it is not fed by a spring.

Then there is the cruise economy. Ships anchor in the caldera and tender passengers ashore below this square. Since 2025 Greece has charged cruise passengers a fee of up to €20 to land here in peak season, and the island has moved to cap cruise arrivals at about 8,000 a day. Some residents call that progress; others say it is a rounding error against a summer day that can put several thousand day-trippers on an island of fifteen thousand.

Two practical things before you walk. Buy a litre and a half of water each here and use a toilet, because the next reliable one is in Imerovigli and after that there is nothing until Oia. And when you leave, stay near the cliff edge — a mapping app will cheerfully send you inland along the main road. Head north out of the square, find the caldera, and climb. The Three Bells church is about a kilometre up the rim.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The square is free. The cable car down to the Old Port cost about €10 one way and €5 for children in 2025, with luggage charged separately — verify the fare at the gate, it changes.
stops.openingHours: The square is open at all hours; cafés, shops and the bus station keep normal daytime hours, with many places closing for the winter.
stops.accessibility: The square itself is paved and level, but everything around it is stepped and steep, and the caldera path north begins with a climb. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Buy all your water here and use a toilet before you start. When you leave the square, ignore any walking route that sends you up the main road: the caldera footpath is roughly a hundred metres west, and it is the whole point of the walk.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the square heading north-west, down through the lanes to the caldera edge, then follow the path north and uphill towards Firostefani. It is about one kilometre, fifteen to twenty minutes, and the first five minutes are the most confusing part of the whole walk: stay close to the cliff, go uphill rather than inland, and ignore any app that points you along the main road. The Three Bells church is a short detour inland and above the path — look for the sign just north of Mama Thira restaurant.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Klearchos Kapoutsis from Santorini, Greece, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: The Three Bells of Fira
stops.narration:
You have climbed a kilometre up the rim, and this is the most photographed church in the Cyclades — and almost everything the postcards tell you about it is wrong. It is called the Three Bells of Fira: a blue dome, a whitewashed body, and three bells in an open arch above the path. Officially it is the Catholic Church of the Dormition, Koimisi tis Theotokou in Greek, and it is Catholic, not Greek Orthodox, which surprises people.

Greece is roughly eight in ten Greek Orthodox. The Orthodox and Catholic churches split in 1054, over the authority of the pope and a handful of doctrinal words, and that schism is still visible on this island. Santorini spent nearly four centuries under Venetian rule after the Fourth Crusade, and a Catholic community stayed; the island still has its own Catholic diocese. This particular church is Greek Byzantine Catholic — in communion with Rome, but worshipping with the Greek liturgy. The site was used by Jesuits before the church was built in 1757, and it has been repaired and extended repeatedly since. Its feast day is 15 August, the Dormition: the day the church remembers Mary being taken up into heaven, which the Orthodox call the Koimisi, the falling asleep.

Now look at the building, because it is a lesson in how the Cyclades are built. The white is lime wash, not paint, and it is not only decorative: lime is a mild disinfectant, it reflects the sun, and it stays porous, so the rain that runs off a lime-washed roof and courtyard is clean enough to catch in a cistern — which is exactly why every traditional house here has a cistern cut into the rock below it. The roof is a barrel vault rather than a flat terrace, because a vault sheds the winter rain and needs no timber, which this island never had enough of. The walls are thick, and many of the buildings around you are not built on the cliff so much as carved into it: pumice is full of trapped gas bubbles, which makes it a natural insulator, warm in winter and cool in summer. Locals call those cave houses yposkafa.

And the blue domes. There are far fewer of them than you think. The postcard shot of a blue dome over a white wall is taken from a handful of churches, over and over, from different angles. Most Cycladic churches are white on white.

One last thing, and it explains why this village looks newer than it should. On 9 July 1956, at 5:11 in the morning, an earthquake of magnitude 7.7 struck south of Amorgos, about fifty kilometres away — the largest earthquake in Greece in the twentieth century. Thirteen minutes later a magnitude 7.2 shock hit close to Santorini. Fifty-three people died, 529 houses on the island were demolished and hundreds more damaged, and a small tsunami reached the beaches. What you are walking through was rebuilt after that, largely in the 1970s and after — and that rebuild is the village the world now photographs.

The bells are a short detour inland, above the caldera path. From here, drop back down to the rim and keep heading north towards Imerovigli.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to look at. It is an active church, not a ticketed site, so if the door happens to be open, step in quietly and leave a coin for its upkeep rather than treating it as an attraction. Nothing here is priced, and the church's own hours move with its calendar — check at the door.
stops.openingHours: The exterior is visible at all hours. The interior opens around services and feast days, and 15 August is its feast day; do not count on getting inside.
stops.accessibility: Reached by a short climb of steps and a lane inland from the caldera path — not step-free, and the churchyard is uneven.
stops.insiderTip: Come before 09:00. The lookout beside the bells is peaceful early and a scrum of tour groups by mid-morning, and the view down the caldera from here is one of the best on the walk.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back down to the caldera path and keep north, climbing steadily. Imerovigli is about 1.3 km on — twenty to thirty minutes, mostly paved and cobbled with a gravel stretch. Aim for the village on the highest point of the rim ahead of you: white houses stacked on the rock, with a large dark headland beyond them.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Imerovigli
stops.narration:
You are now at the highest village on the caldera rim, about 300 metres above the water, and the name tells you its job. Imerovigli comes from imera, day, and vigli, a watch or lookout: a day watchtower, built to spot pirate sails before they reached the island. From here you can see the whole crescent at once — Fira behind you, Oia ahead at the north tip, the two black volcanic islets in the middle of the bay, and Therasia across the water on the far side of the crater.

Those islets are the volcano, and it is not extinct. The caldera you are walking around was made by a colossal eruption around 1600 BC — we will come to that at the next stop — but this bay has been erupting ever since. Palea Kameni, the older islet, first appeared around 47 BC; Nea Kameni, the younger, has been growing since the 1570s and last erupted in 1950. The mechanism is plate tectonics: the African plate is sliding under the Aegean here, and the melting that produces is the reason for the whole South Aegean volcanic arc, a 500-kilometre line of volcanoes running from Methana to Kos. Santorini is its most active centre. In early 2025 the island shook with hundreds of small earthquakes, some above magnitude 5, and people left by ferry and plane as a precaution; the swarm faded. Nobody can tell you when the next eruption comes, only that it will.

Look east, away from the caldera, and you can read the other economy. Those low green bushes laid out in rows are vines, and they do not look like vines because of the wind. Santorini's vines are trained into low basket shapes called kouloura, with the grapes ripening inside a ring of leaves, sheltered from the meltemi — the strong summer north wind — and from the sun. The soil is volcanic ash and pumice over limestone, so poor that the roots go metres down looking for moisture. And because there is no clay in it, the vine louse phylloxera, which destroyed most of Europe's vineyards in the late nineteenth century, cannot survive here: many of these vines are ungrafted and very old, growing on their own roots. The flagship grape is assyrtiko, a white with fierce acidity that survives even when it ripens fully; the sweet wine is vinsanto, made from grapes dried in the sun for two weeks and then aged in oak for at least two years.

The awkward fact is that farming is losing. There are about 1,200 hectares under vine, and the land is worth more as a hotel site. Tourism does not only outbid agriculture for land; it competes for the same water. Which brings us to what is happening to the cliff.

Look at the caldera edge in front of you. Almost every white building is a hotel or a villa, many with a pool cut into a terrace above a 200-metre drop. Cave rooms are excavated into the pumice, sometimes without engineering studies; construction debris and pool water have been dumped down the slope for decades. In August 2025 a section of cliff beside a hotel under construction here in Imerovigli collapsed and sent rock and dust down towards the sea. Days earlier, inspectors had cited the same site for violations, including rooms dug empirically into the volcanic soil and damage to the public path. The collapse was not proved to be caused by those works, but the coincidence made the island's argument concrete: this is a landscape that pays for itself and a landscape being worn out by the paying.

From here the path drops to the left towards the big rock in the water. That is Skaros, and it is worth the detour.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the village. Cafés and small markets charge normal island prices, which are high and rise every season — check the menu before you sit, and expect the tavernas inland from the caldera to be noticeably cheaper than the ones with the view.
stops.openingHours: The lanes are open at all hours. Shops and cafés run through the day and close in the evening, and many shut entirely outside the season.
stops.accessibility: Paved but stepped and steep in places, with narrow lanes, low walls and unprotected drops on the caldera side. Not step-free, and not a place to lose your footing.
stops.insiderTip: This is the last reliable water, toilet and café before Oia — top up here, whatever you think you need. And walk the caldera edge lanes rather than the inland road: the view is the reason you came.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the caldera edge in Imerovigli, follow the signs down to the left towards Skaros. The turn-off is beside the Grace Hotel, and it is about half a kilometre down to the ruins — steep steps and rough path, so count on twenty to thirty minutes down, and a little longer back up.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Zde, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Skaros Rock
stops.narration:
The rock in front of you is a fortress that was also a town. Skaros is a wedge of old lava and pumice jutting west from the rim, and from 1207 it carried one of the five fortified settlements of Venetian Santorini. A Venetian named Giacomo Barozzi built the first castle here — La Roka, the upper castle — under Marco Sanudo, the Venetian who had just made himself Duke of Naxos and handed out the Aegean islands. What grew on the rock was not a fort with a village beside it; it was the village inside the fort: around two hundred houses, cobbled lanes, churches and a garrison, with the sea on three sides and one narrow neck of land to defend. Because it was the largest settlement on the island, Skaros was, in effect, the capital of Venetian Santorini.

Hold on to the strangeness of that. The island's capital was a rock you can walk around in twenty minutes, and its ruling families lived on it because pirates were a real and constant threat. This coast was raided for slaves and cargo by Turkish captains and by the Barbary corsairs out of North Africa, and a castle town on a promontory was the practical answer. Skaros was never taken by the Turks or by pirates. What finished it was geology and politics together: the Ottomans annexed the island in 1566, the pirate threat eased, and the advantages of living on a rock disappeared. Fira, with its harbour and its flat land behind, took over as the capital. Then, in 1650, a submarine volcano called Kolumbo, off the north-east coast of the island, erupted and sent earthquakes and a tsunami across Santorini; part of Skaros is said to have collapsed into the sea. The town emptied through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and by the early 1800s it was ruins.

One building still stands, on the western edge below you: the chapel of Panagia Theoskepasti. Theoskepasti means God-covered — the Virgin who shelters those beneath her cloak — and it is the only structure left on the rock. You can walk down to it, and to the ruins, in about twenty to thirty minutes: steep steps, then a rough path over loose rock, then the same climb back up, which is why the detour costs an hour rather than half of one.

Two honest warnings. The descent is on steps and unstable gravel with drops beside it, so do not do it in flip-flops, in high wind, or in the middle of the day in July or August. And everything you go down, you have to come back up, on legs that still have the rest of the walk in front of them.

If you skip it, you have not missed the point: the whole shape of the rock, the ruins and the chapel are visible from the rim, and the story is the same from up there. Either way, when you leave Imerovigli you leave the last shops, cafés and toilets behind. The next stretch is the wild half.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. There is no gate, no ticket and no facilities — the ruins are open rock, and the chapel below is a working chapel, so treat it as one.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all hours, but only attempt the descent in daylight and dry weather. There is no lighting and no railing on the path.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible, honestly: a steep descent on steps and loose rock, then the same climb back. Around an hour there and back, and the path is exposed to wind.
stops.insiderTip: Do the detour early in the walk, while your legs are fresh and the light is still low. If it is blowing hard or the middle of the day in summer, look at it from the rim instead — the ruins read perfectly well from above.
stops.nextStopDirections: Climb back up to the rim path in Imerovigli and turn north, following the trail signs. The paved lanes end and the path becomes dirt and loose volcanic gravel; after roughly three kilometres you reach the small chapel of Profitis Ilias, where the trail forks. The left fork follows the caldera edge, rougher and more spectacular; the right fork swings inland behind the hill and is easier underfoot. Both lead to Oia.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Zde, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Profitis Ilias Chapel & the Cliff Path
stops.narration:
Now you are on the real thing: dirt and loose volcanic gravel, no shade, no water, and the caldera falling away on your left for the next few kilometres. Somewhere along this stretch you pass a small whitewashed chapel of the Prophet Elijah — Profitis Ilias in Greek — built in 1750, where the trail splits. The left fork keeps to the caldera edge, rougher and more spectacular; the right swings inland behind the hill, easier underfoot. Take the left if you are steady on gravel and the wind is down; take the right if you are not. Both arrive in Oia.

Stand still for a minute and look at the cliff across the water, then at the ground under your feet. Everything here is one event. Around 1600 BC — give or take a century; radiocarbon dating says 1620 to 1530 BC, the archaeologists' pottery dates say later, and the argument is still running — the volcano at the centre of this bay erupted on a scale with no European equivalent. It was a Plinian eruption: a column of ash and gas punched thirty to thirty-five kilometres into the stratosphere, above the weather. On the volcanic explosivity index, which tops out at 8, it scored a 7. The best current estimate is that it threw out twenty-eight to forty-one cubic kilometres of rock and magma. When the magma chamber emptied, the centre of the island collapsed and the sea poured in. That collapse is the caldera — from the Spanish for cauldron, a crater too big to be a crater — and the cliff you are walking along is its inside wall, a stack of ash, pumice and lava hundreds of metres thick. Tsunamis thirty-five to a hundred and fifty metres high hit the north coast of Crete, a hundred and ten kilometres away. Ash three metres deep fell on Anafi, twenty-seven kilometres east.

And here is why this island matters to archaeology. On the south coast, at Akrotiri, stood a Bronze Age town of the Minoan civilisation — the Aegean culture named after the legendary King Minos of Crete, which wrote in the undeciphered script called Linear A. The eruption buried the town in pumice and ash, and because it was buried it survived: three-storey houses, paved streets, huge storage jars called pithoi, and wall paintings of swallows and spring flowers, of blue monkeys, of a fleet of ships with dolphins leaping around it. The town even had running water and stone toilets — the oldest known. Excavation began in 1967 under the archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos and continues, under a large protective roof. And the detail that stops you: no human bodies have ever been found there, and only one gold object, hidden under a floor. The people got out: warned by earthquakes and ash in the weeks before, they took what they could carry and left. Akrotiri is the Pompeii of the Aegean, except that Pompeii's people did not escape.

It is a separate trip, and a good one: a bus from Fira takes about half an hour, the site is covered so it works in the heat, and the finds are in the Museum of Prehistoric Thera in Fira. Tickets have been climbing — around €20 at Akrotiri and €10 at the museum in 2025 — so check at the gate and check the days: the site closes periodically for structural inspections.

One more thing, since you are on a ridge with a view: some writers tie this eruption to Plato's story of Atlantis, the island civilisation that sank beneath the sea. It is a good story, and almost certainly not this island — Plato was writing more than a thousand years later, and he put Atlantis outside the Mediterranean.

Keep going north. Oia is the white smudge on the headland ahead, and it is further than it looks.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free — there is no gate on the trail. The chapel is a working chapel; if it is open, be quiet and leave a coin. The Akrotiri site and the Museum of Prehistoric Thera in Fira charge separately, around €20 and €10 in 2025 — verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: The path is open at all hours, but walk it in daylight only: there is no lighting, no water and no shade on this stretch, and no shelter if the weather turns.
stops.accessibility: Rough, honestly: dirt and loose volcanic gravel, repeated climbs and descents, no handrails and no shade. The inland fork is noticeably easier than the caldera-edge fork, and neither is step-free.
stops.insiderTip: At the fork, choose with the wind, not the map. If the meltemi is blowing hard, take the inland path: the caldera-edge fork is the more beautiful and the more exposed, with loose gravel right at the edge.
stops.nextStopDirections: Keep north on whichever fork you chose. The two paths rejoin, the trail drops to cross a short stretch of roadside near the San Antonio hotel — walk single file and watch for traffic — then climbs once more before the long descent into Oia. It is roughly five and a half kilometres from the chapel, an hour and a half to two hours. You enter the village from the east, past a small market, and then follow the lanes west through the village to the castle at the far end.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Line Lasserre, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Oia Castle (Fort Londsa) at Sunset
stops.narration:
Oia — say it EE-ah — is the village the world has decided Santorini looks like, and the ruin you are standing on is why the view works. This is the castle: the Kasteli of Agios Nikolaos, or Fort Londsa, seat of the Argyri family in the Venetian period and one of the island's five fortified settlements. It is a wreck now, which is the point: no walls block the view, and the panorama takes in the whole caldera, the two volcanic islets, Therasia opposite, and the village stacked below in white terraces. The keep, the goulas, survives in the oldest part of the village, on its south-western edge.

Oia was not always a postcard. In 1890 it was a working seafaring town of about 2,500 residents and 130 sailing ships, carrying wine on the Alexandria-to-Russia run; the two-storey captains' houses are what that money built. Then steamships arrived, shipping concentrated in Piraeus, the trade collapsed, and the island emptied. The 1956 earthquake finished the job: by 1977 Oia had 306 inhabitants.

What you see now is a rescue. In 1976 the Greek National Tourism Organisation put Oia into a programme for the preservation of traditional settlements, run by the architect Aris Konstantinidis; over fifteen years it restored whole clusters of houses and found new uses for them, and the yposkafa — the cave houses the seamen lived in, cut into the pumice — became guesthouses and hotels. The work won a Europa Nostra heritage prize in 1979. So this whitewashed village is a genuine old settlement, saved by being turned into accommodation. That is also the trap it is in.

Because of the sunset. In the last few decades this one hour of the evening became a global product: a photograph everyone recognises, a list everyone wants to tick, and an economy that can charge for it. An hour before sunset the lanes to the castle fill, the steps and rooftops are taken, and as the sun touches the water a crowd applauds. Tables on the caldera side cost thirty to fifty per cent more than the same food two lanes inland. Seen plainly: a village of a few hundred permanent residents absorbing thousands of people a day, most of whom came for fifteen minutes of light.

The bigger argument belongs to the island. Santorini has about fifteen thousand residents and two million visitors a year. Greece now charges cruise passengers up to €20 to come ashore here in peak season and caps cruise arrivals at roughly 8,000 a day; the mayor has argued for tighter limits still. Some residents say tourism is the only thing that has ever paid for this place, and that the alternative is the abandonment Oia had in 1977. Others say water, roads and cliffs cannot carry the load, and the village is being hollowed out into short-let rooms. Both describe the same facts from different ends.

Practical, before the light goes. The sun sets over the water beyond the islets; in mid-September that is a little after seven, and the exact minute moves daily, so check. Below the castle, three hundred steps down, is Ammoudi Bay — the old port, a few tavernas, deep water for swimming, and the same sunset from sea level. The steps are steep and unlit: if you go down, come back up before dark, or eat down there and take a taxi up. And do not walk the cliff path back to Fira after sunset — no lighting, loose gravel. The bus queue in the village will be long, but it will move.

So stand still and let the applause happen around you. You started in a working town square at first light and finish on a ruin in a village that was nearly abandoned twice — and you crossed the crater of a volcano that is only sleeping.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The castle is an open ruin with no gate and no facilities. Everything in the village that has a table, a roof and a view charges for it, and the sunset-view tavernas charge the most.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all hours. The sunset crowd gathers forty-five to sixty minutes before sunset, and the ruins and the lane to them fill up completely.
stops.accessibility: Steps and uneven rock throughout: the castle is a ruin with no railings and drops beside it, and the village lanes are stepped from end to end. Not step-free, and the descent to Ammoudi is three hundred unlit steps.
stops.insiderTip: Watch the sunset from just below the castle, or from a lane with a gap in the buildings, then leave while everyone else is still clapping — the bus queue to Fira is at its worst in the twenty minutes after the sun goes down.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. To get back to Fira, walk east through the village to the bus station and take the bus — it runs late into the evening in season, and the queue right after sunset is long but orderly. Taxis are scarce and should be pre-booked, and a taxi back to Fira costs roughly €20 to €25. If you want the sunset from sea level, the three hundred steps down to Ammoudi Bay start just north of the castle; come back up before dark, or eat down there and take a taxi up. Do not walk the cliff path back to Fira at night.
